1. The animation shows a grid of tiles, one for each monthly start date from January 1991 to July 2016. Each tile is lit (cream) if someone who bought at that start date was ahead of a renter after ten years. It is dark if the renter was ahead. The caption says the data comes from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. It is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. In frame 1, the dark tiles fill the right-hand side of the grid, so many later start dates show the renter ahead. In frames 2 and 3, those dark tiles light up. The new caption reads "lit again: every start 2009 to mid-2016." By frames 3 to 6, nearly every tile is cream. The exceptions are a block of brown (amber) tiles in the middle and a few tiles in the same area that stay cream. The legend lists brown as "renter ahead" but also says "dark: renter ahead," so the amber block is probably the renter-ahead area under a different color.

3. Historically, buying beat renting over ten years for almost every start date in this window, including starts from 2009 to mid-2016. The renter-ahead cases are a limited band of start dates in the middle of the grid, roughly the late-1990s to early-2000s part of the range. The picture also shows that the result depended on when you started.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that buying usually came out ahead over ten-year holds in this history, but the frames don't say that. The footer also says "history, not a forecast."

5. My answer to 4 is my own conclusion. The animation shows the pattern and the "history, not a forecast" caveat, but no on-screen text or picture tells the viewer to buy or rent.
